topics.title: Travelling waves in one dimension
topics.idea: The minus sign in f(z−vt) makes a fixed feature move toward increasing z.
topics.explain: Follow a fixed value of the argument $z-vt$.::A crest keeps its position in the waveform.;;If time increases by Δt, z must increase by vΔt.::This keeps the argument constant.;;Differentiating any smooth f twice gives the wave equation.::The chain rule supplies a factor v² in the time derivative.
topics.trap: A general solution can contain waves in both directions; one sign describes one travelling contribution.
topics.check: Which way does $\cos(2z+6t)$ travel?=>Toward −z at 3 m/s if SI units are used.

topics.title: Sinusoidal waves and phase
topics.idea: A sinusoid repeats in both space and time; k and ω encode those repetitions.
topics.explain: A spatial shift λ must change phase by 2π.::That is one complete cycle.;;A time interval T changes phase by 2π at fixed z.::This defines period and frequency.;;A phase offset δ moves the location of crests but does not change speed.::Speed depends on the ratio ω/k.
topics.trap: Use angular frequency in rad/s with k in rad/m; do not mix ω with ordinary f.
topics.check: If frequency doubles at fixed speed, what happens to λ?=>It halves.

topics.title: Polarization of a wave
topics.idea: Polarization describes the path traced by the transverse electric-field tip at one location.
topics.result: Linear: fixed line; circular: equal perpendicular amplitudes in quadrature; elliptical: general perpendicular components.
topics.explain: Resolve E along two perpendicular transverse directions.::Both are allowed by transversality.;;Equal or opposite phases give a fixed line.::The component ratio is constant.;;A quarter-cycle phase difference with equal amplitudes gives a circle.::Sine and cosine squares sum to one.;;Unequal amplitudes or a general phase difference give an ellipse.::The tip traces a closed tilted curve in the transverse plane.
topics.trap: Handedness labels depend on whether the observer looks with or against propagation; state the viewing convention.
topics.check: Equal amplitudes with zero phase difference: circular or linear?=>Linear, along a 45° line.

topics.title: Maxwell’s vacuum wave equation
topics.idea: Two coupled curl equations predict waves travelling at c.
topics.explain: Take curl of Faraday's law.::This introduces curl B after differentiating in time.;;Use the curl-curl identity and source-free divergence $\nabla\cdot E=0$.::The gradient-of-divergence term vanishes.;;Insert Ampère-Maxwell law.::It replaces curl B by a time derivative of E.;;The two minus signs cancel, leaving the wave equation.::A second time derivative comes from the two coupled laws.
topics.trap: The source-free vacuum derivation does not apply unchanged where charge, current or varying material coefficients are present.

topics.title: Plane-wave geometry and linked fields
topics.idea: In a source-free plane wave, E, B and propagation are mutually perpendicular.
topics.explain: For fields depending on phase $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r-\omega t$, the divergence laws require $\mathbf k\cdot E=\mathbf k\cdot B=0$.::A nonzero oscillatory longitudinal component would have nonzero divergence.;;Faraday's law gives $\mathbf k\times E=\omega B$.::Space and time derivatives share the same sinusoidal factor.;;With $\omega=ck$, B is fixed by E and the travel direction.::The two fields are not independently chosen.
topics.trap: In a travelling vacuum plane wave E and B are in phase, not a quarter-cycle apart.
topics.check: If travel is +z and E points +x at an instant, which way is B?=>+y.

topics.title: Poynting’s theorem
topics.idea: Field energy decreases when it flows outward or does work on charges.
topics.explain: Dot Ampère-Maxwell with E and Faraday with B.::Dot products convert field equations to scalar energy rates.;;Combine them using the divergence identity for $E\times B$.::The curls become an outward-flow term.;;Recognize derivatives of squared fields.::$E\cdot\partial_tE=\partial_t(E^2)/2$.;;Interpret $J\cdot E$ as work per volume per time done on charges.::Electric force transfers field energy to moving charge.
topics.trap: Poynting's vector has units W/m²; energy density has units J/m³.
topics.check: If no current is present and field energy decreases inside a volume, where can it go?=>Through the boundary as outward electromagnetic energy flow.

topics.title: Wave energy and intensity
topics.idea: A vacuum travelling wave has equal electric and magnetic energy densities.
topics.explain: Use $B=E/c$ in $u_B=B^2/(2\mu_0)$.::The plane-wave relation fixes the magnetic amplitude.;;Since $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\epsilon_0$, $u_B=u_E$.::The two field energies are equal.;;Add them and average $\cos^2$ over a cycle.::Intensity is average, not peak, energy flux.
topics.trap: The factor 1/2 is needed for peak amplitude E₀ but not for rms field.
topics.check: If E₀ triples, what happens to intensity?=>It becomes nine times larger.

topics.title: Momentum and radiation pressure
topics.idea: Absorbing or reflecting a wave transfers momentum and therefore exerts force.
topics.result: Vacuum: $g=S/c^2$, momentum=energy/c; normal pressure $p=I/c$ for absorption, $p=2I/c$ for perfect reflection.
topics.explain: An absorbed packet of energy U delivers momentum U/c.::This is the vacuum wave energy-momentum relation.;;Divide transferred momentum by time and area.::Force is momentum transfer rate, and pressure is force per area.;;Perfect reflection reverses the normal momentum.::The momentum change is doubled.
topics.trap: The simple I/c and 2I/c formulas assume normal incidence and the stated ideal surface response.
topics.check: A surface is perfectly reflecting rather than absorbing. At equal incident I, pressure changes how?=>It doubles.

topics.title: Waves in linear media
topics.idea: A homogeneous lossless nondispersive medium changes speed and field ratios.
topics.explain: Use D=εE and B=μH in source-free macroscopic Maxwell equations.::Constitutive constants describe the medium.;;Repeat the vacuum curl-curl derivation to obtain $\nabla^2E=\mu\epsilon\partial_t^2E$.::Uniform coefficients can be taken outside derivatives.;;The speed follows by comparison with the wave equation.::Its coefficient is $1/v^2$.;;For a travelling plane wave, intensity is $E_0^2/(2\eta)$ and $S=E\times H$.::H replaces B/μ₀ in the macroscopic energy flux.
topics.trap: Conduction, absorption, dispersion or anisotropy require a more general treatment. Vacuum momentum/pressure relations are not automatically transferable inside matter.
topics.check: For $\mu_r=1$ and $\epsilon_r=4$, find v and η relative to vacuum.=>$v=c/2$ and $\eta=\eta_0/2$.

questions.prompt: Determine the direction and speed of $f(z,t)=A\cos(4z+12t)$, with SI coordinates.
questions.answer: Keep $4z+12t$ constant: $4\,dz/dt+12=0$, so $dz/dt=-3$ m/s. A constant-phase point travels toward decreasing z.
questions.final: Speed 3 m/s toward −z.

questions.prompt: Write the one-dimensional wave equation and interpret its two derivatives.
questions.answer: $\partial_z^2f=v^{-2}\partial_t^2f$. The left side is spatial curvature; the right side is time acceleration divided by speed squared. It constrains how a disturbance propagates, rather than specifying one particular shape.
questions.final: $\partial_t^2f=v^2\partial_z^2f$.

questions.prompt: A vacuum wave has f=100 MHz. Find λ, k and ω.
questions.answer: $\lambda=c/f=3.00$ m; $k=2\pi/\lambda=2.094$ rad/m; $\omega=2\pi f=6.283\times10^8$ rad/s. MHz means $10^6$ Hz.
questions.final: λ=3.00 m, k=2.094 rad/m, $\omega=6.283\times10^8$ rad/s.

questions.prompt: Two points along a sinusoidal wave are separated by λ/4. What is their phase difference at the same time?
questions.answer: $\Delta\phi=k\Delta z=(2\pi/\lambda)(\lambda/4)=\pi/2$ radians. They are a quarter-cycle apart; which leads depends on the ordered positions and propagation direction.
questions.final: Phase separation magnitude $\pi/2$.

questions.prompt: Define polarization and explain why a vacuum plane EM wave can be polarized.
questions.answer: Polarization specifies the motion of the E-field tip in the plane transverse to propagation at a fixed point. Two independent transverse components can have different amplitudes and phase relations, giving different polarization states.
questions.final: Polarization concerns transverse E orientation and its time evolution.

questions.prompt: What amplitude and phase conditions produce circular polarization from two perpendicular components?
questions.answer: The components have equal nonzero amplitudes and phase difference $\pm\pi/2$ modulo $2\pi$. The magnitude of E is then constant while its tip rotates. Zero phase difference instead gives a straight line.
questions.final: Equal perpendicular amplitudes in quadrature give a circle.

questions.prompt: Classify $E_x=3\cos\phi$ and $E_y=4\cos\phi$. Give peak magnitude and orientation.
questions.answer: The component ratio is $E_y/E_x=4/3$, constant whenever defined. The tip moves on a line at $\tan^{-1}(4/3)=53.13^\circ$ to +x. Peak magnitude is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ in the field units.
questions.final: Linear polarization, peak 5, line angle 53.13°.

questions.prompt: Classify $E_x=3\cos\phi$, $E_y=4\sin\phi$ and write the tip's locus.
questions.answer: Eliminate phase using $\cos^2\phi+\sin^2\phi=1$. This gives $E_x^2/9+E_y^2/16=1$, an ellipse with semi-axes 3 and 4. The fields are in quadrature but amplitudes differ.
questions.final: Elliptical polarization.

questions.prompt: How does Maxwell theory predict the speed of waves in vacuum?
questions.answer: The source-free curl equations give $\nabla^2E=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2E$. Comparing with the wave equation gives $c=(\mu_0\epsilon_0)^{-1/2}\simeq3.00\times10^8$ m/s.
questions.final: Vacuum wave speed is determined by μ₀ and ε₀.

questions.prompt: State the assumptions needed for the elementary vacuum EM wave equation.
questions.answer: The region is vacuum with no free or bound charges/currents, so ρ=0, J=0, D=ε₀E and B=μ₀H. The vacuum constants are uniform and the fields are differentiable. Sources may exist outside the region.
questions.final: The derivation applies locally in a source-free vacuum region.

questions.prompt: A wave travels along +x and E points +z at an instant. Which way does B point?
questions.answer: $B=(1/c)\hat x\times E$. Since $\hat x\times\hat z=-\hat y$, B points −y. The check is $E\times B=\hat z\times(-\hat y)=+\hat x$.
questions.final: B points −y.

questions.prompt: A vacuum plane wave has electric peak 300 V/m. Find its magnetic peak and relative phase.
questions.answer: $B_0=E_0/c=300/(3.00\times10^8)=1.00\times10^{-6}$ T. E and B reach their signed extrema together for a travelling plane wave; they are in phase.
questions.final: $B_0=1.00$ μT, in phase with E.

questions.prompt: What does transverse mean for a vacuum plane electromagnetic wave?
questions.answer: Both $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ are perpendicular to the propagation vector k: $k\cdot E=k\cdot B=0$. They are also perpendicular to one another. Their oscillations are not along the travel direction.
questions.final: E, B and k form mutually perpendicular directions.

questions.prompt: Define the vacuum Poynting vector and state its physical meaning and SI unit.
questions.answer: $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0$. It describes electromagnetic power flow per unit area, directed along energy transport. Its units are W/m².
questions.final: S is an energy flux density.

questions.prompt: Interpret positive $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ in Poynting’s theorem.
questions.answer: Positive $J\cdot E$ means the field does work on charges at that power per unit volume. It removes electromagnetic field energy locally unless replenished by inflow. In an ohmic resistor it equals $\sigma E^2$.
questions.final: Positive $J\cdot E$ transfers field energy to matter.

questions.prompt: In a vacuum travelling plane wave, compare electric and magnetic energy densities.
questions.answer: $u_E=\epsilon_0E^2/2$. Using $B=E/c$ and $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\epsilon_0$ gives $u_B=B^2/(2\mu_0)=u_E$. Equality holds instantaneously for this travelling plane wave.
questions.final: Each field stores half the total wave energy density.

questions.prompt: Express the average intensity of a vacuum sinusoidal wave using peak and rms electric fields.
questions.answer: $I=\frac12\epsilon_0cE_0^2$ and $I=\epsilon_0cE_{\rm rms}^2$, with $E_{\rm rms}=E_0/\sqrt2$. The half comes from the cycle average of cosine squared.
questions.final: Use the half only with peak amplitude.

questions.prompt: What is the pressure on an ideal absorbing surface at normal incidence from a vacuum beam of intensity I?
questions.answer: An absorbed energy U brings momentum U/c. Per time and area, this gives $p=I/c$. The result assumes complete absorption and normal incidence; its units are N/m².

questions.prompt: Why does an ideal reflector have twice the normal radiation pressure of an ideal absorber at the same incident intensity?
questions.answer: An incident momentum component +U/c becomes −U/c after reflection, so the surface gains 2U/c. Absorption gains only U/c. Dividing by area and time gives $p=2I/c$.
questions.final: Momentum reversal doubles the transfer.

questions.prompt: A lossless nonmagnetic dielectric has $\epsilon_r=2.25$. Find refractive index and wave speed.
questions.answer: $n=\sqrt{\mu_r\epsilon_r}=\sqrt{2.25}=1.5$. Thus $v=c/n=2.00\times10^8$ m/s. This uses a homogeneous nondispersive scalar permittivity and μr=1.
questions.final: n=1.5 and $v=2.00\times10^8$ m/s.

questions.prompt: Show directly that any twice-differentiable $f(z-vt)$ solves the one-dimensional wave equation.
questions.answer: Set $s=z-vt$. Then $\partial_z f=f'(s)$ and $\partial_z^2f=f''(s)$.::The derivative of s with respect to z is one.;;$\partial_tf=-vf'(s)$ and $\partial_t^2f=v^2f''(s)$.::Each time derivative contributes −v.;;Thus $\partial_t^2f=v^2\partial_z^2f$.::Both sides equal $v^2f''(s)$.;;The shape is unchanged as s remains constant along z=vt+constant.::This also explains the direction of propagation.
questions.final: Every smooth profile f(z−vt) is a right-travelling solution.

questions.prompt: Write E for a +z travelling, x-polarized vacuum wave with peak 20 V/m and wavelength 0.60 m, whose field is maximum at z=t=0. Find B.
questions.answer: $k=2\pi/0.60=10.472$ rad/m and $\omega=ck=3.142\times10^9$ rad/s.::Vacuum dispersion is $\omega=ck$.;;Choose cosine with zero phase: $E=20\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat x$.::Cosine is one at the specified origin.;;$B=(20/c)\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat y$.::Use the right-handed plane-wave relation.;;$B_0=6.667\times10^{-8}$ T.::Electric and magnetic amplitudes differ by c.
questions.final: $E=20\cos(10.472z-3.142\times10^9t)\hat x$ V/m; B has the same phase and +y direction.

questions.prompt: For $E_x=a\cos\phi$ and $E_y=b\cos(\phi+\delta)$, derive the polarization ellipse equation.
questions.answer: Set $X=E_x/a=\cos\phi$ and $Y=E_y/b=\cos\phi\cos\delta-\sin\phi\sin\delta$.::Expand the cosine of a sum.;;Rearrange $Y-X\cos\delta=-\sin\phi\sin\delta$.::Isolate the sine term.;;Square and use $\sin^2\phi=1-X^2$.::Eliminate the phase.;;Collect terms: $X^2+Y^2-2XY\cos\delta=\sin^2\delta$.::This is the general conic relation.;;For δ=0 or π it degenerates to a line; for equal a,b and δ=±π/2 it is a circle.::These are limiting phase and amplitude choices.
questions.final: $E_x^2/a^2+E_y^2/b^2-2E_xE_y\cos\delta/(ab)=\sin^2\delta$.

questions.prompt: At z=0 take $E_x=E_0\cos\omega t$, $E_y=E_0\sin\omega t$. Describe its rotation as viewed from +z looking toward the origin. Avoid an unqualified handedness label.
questions.answer: At t=0 the tip is on +x.::Cosine is one and sine zero.;;At T/4 it is on +y, at T/2 on −x and at 3T/4 on −y.::Advance the phase by π/2 each quarter-cycle.;;Viewed from +z toward the origin, +x to +y is counterclockwise.::This is the standard xy-plane orientation from its positive normal.;;The magnitude is $\sqrt{E_x^2+E_y^2}=E_0$.::Sine and cosine squares add to one.
questions.final: Circular motion, counterclockwise from the explicitly stated +z viewpoint.

questions.final: $\nabla^2E=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2E$.

questions.final: $\nabla^2B=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2B$.

questions.prompt: For $E=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat x$, use Faraday’s law to derive B for a vacuum travelling wave.
questions.answer: The y component of curl E is $\partial_zE_x=-kE_0\sin(kz-\omega t)$.::Only Eₓ varies, and only along z.;;Try $B=B_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat y$, so $-\partial_tB_y=-\omega B_0\sin(kz-\omega t)$.::The time derivative of cosine contributes +ω before Faraday's minus sign.;;Equate amplitudes: $kE_0=\omega B_0$.::Both sides have the same phase factor.;;Since $\omega/k=c$, $B_0=E_0/c$.::Use vacuum dispersion.
questions.final: B points +y, is in phase, and has peak E₀/c.

questions.prompt: Someone proposes a +z vacuum wave with E along +x and B along +y but $B_0=2E_0/c$. Can the pair satisfy Maxwell’s equations? Explain.
questions.answer: Its directions pass the right-hand test, but direction alone is insufficient.::The fields must satisfy the curl equations.;;Faraday's law requires $kE_0=\omega B_0$.::Derivatives connect the amplitudes.;;Vacuum wave dispersion requires $\omega=ck$, hence $B_0=E_0/c$.::Both conditions must hold together.;;The proposed factor two violates this unless both amplitudes vanish.::A nonzero source-free travelling pair has a fixed ratio.
questions.final: No: the proposed amplitude ratio violates Maxwell's curl equations.

questions.prompt: A region loses field energy at 5 W while charges inside receive 2 W from the field. Find the net outward electromagnetic power.
questions.answer: Integrate Poynting's theorem: $dU/dt+P_{\rm out}=-P_{\rm matter}$.::The divergence theorem converts S to boundary flow.;;Here $dU/dt=-5$ W and $P_{\rm matter}=+2$ W.::Loss of stored energy carries a negative derivative.;;Thus $-5+P_{\rm out}=-2$, giving $P_{\rm out}=3$ W.::Part of the released energy goes to matter and the remainder leaves the region.
questions.final: Net outward power is 3 W.

questions.prompt: A vacuum plane wave has $E_0=100$ V/m. Calculate mean energy density and intensity.
questions.answer: $\langle u\rangle=\epsilon_0E_0^2/2=(8.854\times10^{-12})(10^4)/2=4.427\times10^{-8}$ J/m³.::The average squared cosine is 1/2.;;$I=c\langle u\rangle=13.28$ W/m².::A travelling wave carries its energy at c.;;Equivalently $I=E_0^2/(2\eta_0)$ with $\eta_0\simeq376.7$ Ω.::This provides an independent ratio check.
questions.final: Mean energy density $4.427\times10^{-8}$ J/m³; intensity 13.28 W/m².

questions.prompt: A uniform vacuum beam carries 2 W through area $1.0\times10^{-4}$ m². Find intensity and peak E and B.
questions.answer: $I=P/A=2.0\times10^4$ W/m².::Power is uniformly distributed.;;$E_0=\sqrt{2I/(\epsilon_0c)}=3.881\times10^3$ V/m.::Invert the peak-field intensity relation.;;$B_0=E_0/c=1.294\times10^{-5}$ T.::The wave is in vacuum.;;The square root is essential because intensity depends on field squared.::Doubling power does not double field amplitude.

questions.prompt: A 3 W beam hits a surface normally in vacuum. Find force for complete absorption and perfect reflection.
questions.answer: Incident energy per second is P, so incident momentum per second is P/c.::A vacuum wave has momentum U/c.;;Absorption gives $F=P/c=1.0\times10^{-8}$ N.::All incident momentum is retained.;;Reflection gives $F=2P/c=2.0\times10^{-8}$ N.::Normal momentum reverses.;;Both forces point into the surface along the incoming beam.::The surface receives forward momentum.
questions.final: Absorber: 10 nN; reflector: 20 nN.

questions.prompt: At normal incidence a surface reflects fraction R of a vacuum beam's intensity and absorbs the remainder, with no transmission. Derive its pressure.
questions.answer: The absorbed fraction $(1-R)I$ transfers pressure $(1-R)I/c$.::Absorbed momentum is removed from the beam.;;The reflected fraction RI transfers $2RI/c$.::Reflection reverses its normal momentum.;;Add contributions: $p=(1+R)I/c$.::Power fractions are mutually exclusive.;;R=0 and R=1 recover the absorbing and reflecting limits.::Check the result against known endpoints.
questions.final: $p=(1+R)I/c$ for no transmission at normal incidence.

questions.target: Impedance and field ratio in medium
questions.prompt: A lossless homogeneous medium has $\epsilon_r=4$, $\mu_r=1$ and electric peak 60 V/m. Find speed, impedance, B₀, H₀ and intensity.
questions.answer: $v=c/2=1.50\times10^8$ m/s and $\eta=\eta_0/2\simeq188.4$ Ω.::Use the square-root constitutive relations.;;$B_0=E_0/v=4.0\times10^{-7}$ T and $H_0=E_0/\eta=0.3185$ A/m.::The ratios are B/E=1/v and E/H=η.;;$I=E_0^2/(2\eta)=9.555$ W/m².::Average the product of in-phase sinusoidal E and H.

questions.prompt: A 600 nm vacuum wave enters a stationary transparent nonmagnetic medium with n=1.5. Find f, v and wavelength inside. Explain which quantity stays fixed.
questions.answer: Vacuum frequency is $f=c/\lambda_0=5.0\times10^{14}$ Hz.::Convert nm to metres.;;Frequency stays the same across a stationary boundary.::The boundary fields must match at every instant.;;$v=c/n=2.0\times10^8$ m/s, so $\lambda=v/f=400$ nm.::Use the unchanged f with the reduced speed.
questions.final: f=$5.0\times10^{14}$ Hz remains fixed; v=$2.0\times10^8$ m/s; λ=400 nm.

questions.target: Energy transport speed in linear medium
questions.prompt: Show that S=vu for a travelling plane wave in a homogeneous linear lossless nondispersive medium.
questions.answer: $u=(\epsilon E^2+\mu H^2)/2$.::Both field energies are reversible under the stated assumptions.;;Since $H=E/\eta$ and $\eta^2=\mu/\epsilon$, $\mu H^2=\epsilon E^2$, hence $u=\epsilon E^2$.::The wave's electric and magnetic energy shares are equal.;;$S=EH=E^2/\eta$.::The fields are perpendicular and form a travelling wave.;;$S/u=1/(\epsilon\eta)=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}=v$.::Substitute the impedance definition.
questions.final: $\mathbf S=vu\hat k$ under the stated nondispersive lossless assumptions.

abla^2E=\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t^2E$.::The fields are source-free vacuum fields.;;A cosine of phase $k\cdot r-\omega t$ then requires $\omega^2=c^2k^2$, with $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$.::Second derivatives supply −k² and −ω².;;The divergence laws give $k\cdot E_0=k\cdot B_0=0$.::The oscillatory fields have no longitudinal component.;;Faraday gives $k	imes E_0=\omega B_0$, hence $B_0=(1/c)\hat k	imes E_0$.::The curl law fixes orientation, amplitude and phase.;;For travel +z choose E along x and B along y with the same cosine.::Then E cross B points along propagation.

questions.final: Poynting's theorem balances stored energy, boundary energy flux and mechanical/electrical work on charge.

questions.target: Wave energy momentum and pressure synthesis
questions.prompt: Derive the vacuum plane-wave energy/intensity relations and use momentum transport to explain radiation pressure for an absorber and reflector.
questions.answer: The plane-wave amplitude relation gives $u_B=u_E=\epsilon_0E^2/2$.::Substitute B=E/c into magnetic energy.;;Total $u=\epsilon_0E^2$ and $S=cu\hat k$.::Compute the Poynting vector.;;For sinusoidal peak E₀, $I=\epsilon_0cE_0^2/2$.::Average cosine squared.;;Vacuum momentum density is $g=S/c^2$, so momentum carried by energy U is U/c.::Divide energy density by c.;;For normal complete absorption, momentum delivered per time per area gives $p=I/c$.::Pressure is momentum flux.;;Perfect reflection reverses the normal momentum and gives $p=2I/c$.::The momentum change is twice the incoming value.;;These formulas refer to vacuum incident waves and ideal stated surface behaviour.::Inside material, field/matter momentum requires additional care.
questions.final: Energy and momentum transport jointly predict measurable radiation pressure.

questions.prompt: Derive the wave equation and field ratios in a source-free homogeneous linear lossless nondispersive medium, and identify the limits of the model.
questions.answer:
Use $D=\epsilon E$, $B=\mu H$, with no free current or charge.::Constitutive laws specify an isotropic linear medium.;;Then $
abla	imes E=-\mu\partial_tH$ and $
